title: Traffic Prioritization & Quota Simulator — Walkthrough | BlueOrchid Technologies
summary: Redwood AE+SE demo of console quota simulator and API routing policies. Focus on org/project key model, traffic prioritization, and how quota slices/fairburst work under mixed workloads. Customer asked about SSO/KMS, data residency, and cost tradeoffs for Dedicated vs Hosted. Agreed next steps: send pilot pricing, security pack, and set up a sandbox trial with two tenant profiles for a short POC.

transcript:
Meeting header:
Date: 2025-10-01
Start: 15:00 PDT
Duration: ~47 minutes
Recording id: ff-20251001-az3b9
Shared links: redwood-console-playbook.pdf, redwood-security-pack.zip, sandbox-access.redwood.io (shared during call)

[00:00] Liam Ortiz: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. I'm Liam, AE on the account, with Priya our solutions engineer and Oscar from CS. How's everyone doing?
[00:06] Elena Park: Good, thanks. We've got a short agenda — we want to see the quota simulator in action and understand routing rules for our multi-tenant platform.
[00:12] Liam Ortiz: Great. Priya will drive the demo. Quick callout, we'll show the Console simulator and then a brief API pattern for org/project keys and how traffic prioritization is enforced.
[00:20] Priya Nambiar: All right pulling up the Console now. Can you all see my screen? (pause) Cool. So here is the new "Quota Simulator" tab inside Redwood Console — it's intentionally interactive.
[00:30] [00:30] Priya Nambiar: First, I create two tenants, Tenant A (free tier) and Tenant B (premium). I'm going to attach an org key at the org level and project keys for different app surfaces. Notice the key hierarchy — org keys can carry global quotas and project keys inherit or override.
[00:48] Marcus Li: Quick Q — if we put a global org quota and then project-level overrides, which wins?
[00:52] Priya Nambiar: The simulator shows precedence: project > org > default. So project-level caps and concurrency can carve out or extend org rules. There's also a sticky routing flag which keeps session traffic on the same project key under sticky lanes.
[01:10] Tom Anders: Does sticky routing impact failover? If a node or model goes down, what's the fallback?
[01:14] Priya Nambiar: Good question. Fallbacks are policy-based. You can set fallback to another model variant or to a lower-cost region; the request will dequeue from the sticky lane and be routed according to your priority tiers. There is a short backoff to prevent thundering herd.
[01:28] [01:28] Priya Nambiar: Now I'm going to run a simulated workload. The simulator accepts a CSV or you can pick a prebuilt profile — I'm selecting "mixed-burst-profile-500qps". It'll run a 10-minute equivalent and show token-cost, tail latency, and percentage of requests throttled per key.
[01:44] [01:44] (sim click noises)
[01:46] Priya Nambiar: All right it's running — you can see the visual timeline: green for served, orange for queued, red for rejected. Tenant A, the free tier, gets a smaller slice per the org policy; Tenant B gets a guaranteed reservation plus burst headroom.
[02:02] Elena Park: Can we change the burst window? We have traffic spikes for critical product flows and want short, high-priority windows.
[02:07] Priya Nambiar: Yes — we have a "burst window" parameter and a "fairburst" algorithm. Fairburst spreads burst capacity by recent usage and priority score; it prevents a single noisy tenant from taking all headroom.
[02:20] [02:20] Marcus Li: That sounds like leaky bucket but smarter?
[02:22] Priya Nambiar: Exactly, it's leaky-bucket-inspired with priority weighting and decay. You can tune decay interval to match your traffic burstiness.
[02:28] [02:28] Liam Ortiz: I want to highlight cost tradeoffs here — if you reserve a larger committed capacity in Dedicated you get predictable throughput and lower per-token cost, but Hosted with adaptive burst can keep cost low on variable workloads. We usually model expected QPS against unit economics in Redwood Optimize.
[02:44] [02:44] Aisha Rahman: On the security side — how is audit logging handled for key-level operations and what about KMS integration? We need full key rotation and separation of control plane logs from inference logs.
[02:54] Oscar Ruiz: Redwood stores audit logs in a separate append-only stream; you can stream logs to customer S3 or your SIEM. For encryption, we support AWS KMS and customer-managed Cloud HSM in Private deployments. Key rotation is supported via staged key rollovers. We'll share the security pack.
[03:12] [03:12] Priya Nambiar: For the simulator I'm toggling in a scenario where an encrypted org key is used with KMS. You'll notice the "audit events" column — each token request resolves key metadata and logs the key id, project id, and route decisions.
[03:28] Tom Anders: How granular are routing policies? Could we route certain endpoints to a cheaper model but critical endpoints to a higher SLO cluster?
[03:34] Priya Nambiar: Yes — you can route by route tag, latency budget, or by explicit intent annotation in the request. E.g., header X-req-priority: high. Policies are first-class in Console and can be attached to keys or projects.
[03:50] [03:50] Priya Nambiar: I'm switching to the API pattern view — this is what an org key request looks like. We include project_id in metadata, prefer header-based routing, and the server returns a routing decision and quota token. If quota is exhausted, you'll either get 429 or a queue token depending on your queuing policy.
[04:10] Marcus Li: About the queue — is that client-visible? Can we set retry/backoff recommendations?
[04:14] Priya Nambiar: The queue is server-side but we provide a token to the client that can be used to poll or receive a streaming update. We recommend exponential backoff + jitter. The simulator can emit client-side metrics to validate retry patterns.
[04:30] [04:30] Elena Park: We have strict residency needs for EU customers. Does the quota enforcement happen in region, or is it global?
[04:36] Liam Ortiz: You can pin policies by region. For Private deployments and VPC options, enforcement happens in-region. For Hosted, you can select region affinity for traffic and enforce per-region quotas.
[04:52] [04:52] Priya Nambiar: Back to simulator results — you can export a CSV of rejected requests and their reasons. I'm toggling a scenario where Tenant B's premium SLA is honored; the GUI highlights the preemptions — lower-priority queued requests get dropped in favor of premium tokens once a capacity reclaim happens.
[05:12] Tom Anders: Can we see a canary rollout pattern for policy changes? We want to test new quotas with 5% traffic first.
[05:16] Priya Nambiar: Yep — Console supports canary rollouts for policy changes. You create a rule and deploy with a percent rollout. The simulator can approximate steady-state after the canary.
[05:28] [05:28] Liam Ortiz: Wanted to call out an integration pattern: if you have an API gateway in front, we recommend issuing short-lived project keys to the gateway and exchanging them for org/session tokens — gives you better attribution and easier rotation.
[05:42] Elena Park: That helps for our gateway flow. One more Q on observability: how are token-level costs reported?
[05:48] Oscar Ruiz: In Redwood Console billing reports you get token-level breakdowns by key, model, and route. There's also a latency-cost scatter that helps identify expensive tails.
[05:58] [05:58] Priya Nambiar: I'm now flipping to a simulated incident: region us-west is degraded. Watch how the traffic is steered: high-priority lanes go to us-east warm cluster, others either queue or drop depending on policy. The timeline shows an uptick in latency but no SLO breach for premium lanes.
[06:20] Marcus Li: For our POC we need a controlled failover test. Can the sandbox simulate a node death?
[06:24] Priya Nambiar: Yes, the sandbox can inject faults, network egress loss, or model hot restart. We'll set up a test with controlled chaos.
[06:34] [06:34] (brief cross-talk)
[06:40] Aisha Rahman: On compliance — you'll share SOC2 artifacts and a dataflow diagram? We also need to confirm logs retention and deletion capabilities.
[06:48] Oscar Ruiz: We'll upload the SOC2 summary and a recommended retention policy. For Private deployments, retention can be customer-controlled. For Hosted, we provide retention windows with export hooks.
[06:58] [06:58] Priya Nambiar: Wrapping up the sim — I changed the project-level concurrency from 50 to 200 and re-ran the burst profile. You can see cost delta in the right-hand panel. It gives a projected monthly spend for the simulated profile.
[07:14] Tom Anders: Do we get an API to programmatically adjust quotas for autoscaling?
[07:17] Priya Nambiar: Yes, there's a Quota API. You can update slices, create temporary overrides, and tear them down. We also have webhook hooks for quota alarms.
[07:28] [07:28] Liam Ortiz: Time check — about 20 minutes left. Any other deep technical asks before we move to next steps?
[07:34] Marcus Li: We'd like a short runbook for incident playbooks around quota exhaustion — what to do if a noisy neighbor floods a shard.
[07:38] Priya Nambiar: We'll include a runbook template in the sandbox repo. It includes steps: identify offending key, apply emergency dampening rule, create a targeted canary rollback, and notify via pager hook.
[07:52] [07:52] (Typing sounds)
[08:00] Elena Park: One practical ask — in our compliance review, our legal team will ask about data separation between control plane and inference logs. Simple answer?
[08:06] Oscar Ruiz: Control plane logs are separate and can be exported. Inference logs can be configured to not persist content tokens; we also support token redaction at rest. We'll include specifics in the security pack.
[08:20] [08:20] Priya Nambiar: Ok final part — pilot scoping. For a 4-week pilot we suggest two tenant profiles: 1) simulated free+burst traffic; 2) premium flows with steady QPS and SLO targets. We'll instrument with the simulator and run a controlled failover. Outcome: validate latency SLOs, cost projections, and routing behavior.
[08:44] Tom Anders: That sounds fair. What would you need from us?
[08:46] Liam Ortiz: Short list: sample traffic CSV, auth flow details, SLO targets, and a contact for access. We'll provision sandbox and give you a playbook.
[08:56] [08:56] Elena Park: We'll send the CSV and SLOs by next week.
[09:00] Priya Nambiar: Great, I'll schedule the sandbox provision step.
[09:04] [09:04] Liam Ortiz: Any competitors we should be comparing against in the pilot? We can model similar quotas in Anthropic's or OpenAI's endpoints but Redwood's advantage is the unified routing + embedded simulator.
[09:18] Marcus Li: We'll compare to our current homegrown shaper and a short benchmark vs OpenAI.
[09:22] [09:22] Liam Ortiz: Perfect. Let's recap next steps.
[09:26] (recap)
[09:26] Liam Ortiz: 1) Liam send pricing/pilot SOW by Friday; 2) Priya set up sandbox and provisioning; 3) Customer sends sample traffic and SLOs; 4) Oscar shared security docs now.
[09:40] Elena Park: Thanks — that works.
[09:42] [09:42] (call wrap-up small talk)
[09:50] Liam Ortiz: Thanks everyone — we'll follow up in email with links.

Notes on transcript: occasional ASR errors present — model names sometimes transcribed as "red wood" or "fair burst" as two words. Speaker attributions may shift at times (Priya/Liam overlap).

End of recording.
